en: Having bowed his head in purity to Prajāpati, the lord of the age consisting of five years, whose limbs are the days, seasons, solstices,
and months; having bowed his head to Time and saluted Sarasvatī.
I shall proclaim the knowledge of time belonging to the high-souled Lagadha;
I shall explain the entire course of the luminaries in due order—
that which is esteemed in the world by the Brahmins for the successful accomplishment of the purpose of sacrificial times.

The period known as *gatasaṃjñika* consists of twelve half-years doubled (twenty-four years), increased by sixty times sixty; this is said to be the total number of *parvas*. When the Moon and the Sun, together with Indra, simultaneously ascend through the vowels.
The Yuga begins with that [month], namely Māgha; Tapas (Phālguna) is the bright fortnight, and the northern solstice indeed occurs then.
At the beginning of Śraviṣṭhā, the sun and the moon both enter the north;
however, at the midpoint of Āśleṣā, the sun always moves southward during the months of Māgha and Śrāvaṇa.
The increase of heat is one *prastha* of water during the northern course, while there is a decrease at night;
in the southern course, these two are reversed. However, by means of the six-muhūrta transit, they say the seventh [increase] is double, and the thirteenth is the first of the transits (*ayana*).
The fourth and tenth [houses], as well as the first two of each pair [of signs], are auspicious even during the *bahula* (dark) fortnight of the menstrual cycle.

Vasu, Tvaṣṭṛ, Bhava, Aja, Mitra, the Sarpas, the Aśvins, Jala, Dhātṛ, and Ka are the lords of the months starting from the northern solstice (*ayana*), while the season (*ṛtu*) corresponds to the fifth sign from the sign occupied by the Moon.
The degrees (bhāṃśāḥ) arising from the twelve fortnights should be divided by eight;

[the result] multiplied by eleven and diminished [by one], provided it is the bright fortnight. And if it is the dark fortnight, half [should be subtracted]. In place of the eight degrees, nineteen minutes (kalā) should be applied.
In the case of a deficient position, one should add seventy-three; [the results] are equal to the deficiency.
The remainder of the signs is a third part, and the portion of the days is a fourteenth part;
having subtracted the fractional part, when more than half has passed, the subsequent portion is known by the experts as two, one, and one for the highest [result].
After fifteen days of the lunar fortnight have passed, one should indicate that [the portion] has been consumed.
However, the portion that has risen [again] would consist of nine [days], increased by two deficient portions.

One should know that the [nakṣatras] beginning with Revatī, Mṛgaśiras, Svāti, Āpa (Āśleṣā), Aja (Pūrvaphalgunī), Kṛttikā, and the eldest (Uttaraphalgunī) are associated with the signs by their characteristics.
One should understand them as equal in their eastern halves during the subsequent lunar nodes;
the commencement occurs on the fourteenth day, and the divisions of the quarters are determined by the deities.
Ten and twenty *kalās* constitute two *nāḍikās* of a *muhūrta*.
Thirty of those *kalās* of a day, however, would amount to six hundred and three. Two *nāḍikās* are one *muhūrta*; fifty *palas* are one *āḍhaka*.
From an āḍhaka, a droṇa consists of three kuṭapas;
a bhāra consists of seven droṇas. Soma has twelve [months], the sun has thirteen days, and the nakṣatras are nine. Five syllables are traditionally known as a kāṣṭhā.

One should indicate the elapsed asterisms by multiplying those [from Śraviṣṭhā] by six; one should know the elapsed months by multiplying them by twelve, and the lunar seasons by multiplying them by two. One should subtract the doubled lunar day from the elapsed portions of the parvan.
In those portions of the mandala, the sun reaches its culmination on the lunar days (tithis).
One should add the lunar day multiplied by seven to those digits of the commencement of the parvan; that sum, indeed, one should know as the digits of the commencement (ādānikī-kalā).
Whatever portion remains from the northern course that has been traversed, when compared to the remainder of the southern course,

and is divided by sixty-one and doubled, it shall be twelve [units] as the measure of the day. Half of this, which is always [the case] at every lunar festival (parvan), constitutes the division of the day.

One should know the remainder of the seasons by calculating them together with the [remaining] parvans. Thus is the summary of the method; furthermore, one should calculate the days and divide that which has been practiced within the mass of objects to be known by the mass of knowledge.
Agni, Prajāpati, Soma, Rudra, Aditi, Bṛhaspati,
the serpents, the ancestors, Bhaga, and Aryaman;
Savitṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, Indra and Agni, and Mitra as well.
Indra, Nirṛti, and the Waters, as well as the Viśvedevas;
Viṣṇu, the Vasus, Varuṇa, and likewise Aja Ekapād;
Ahirbudhnya, Pūṣan, the two Aśvins, and Yama as well. (26–27)

"These are the deities of the lunar mansions (nakṣatra); by means of these, in the performance of the sacrifice, the name of the sacrificer born under a particular mansion is traditionally recorded by those learned in the scriptures. In this manner, [the names] of months, years, auspicious moments (muhūrta), and festivals [are determined]."
Lagadha spoke the exposition on the days, seasons, solstices, and the limbs [of the year], as well as the conduct of the moon and sun, the world, and what is esteemed in the world;
the learned man who knows the conduct of the moon and sun, being a knower of the Vedas, attains [the goal]. (29–30)
The equinox (viṣuva) is multiplied by that [number], then diminished by two and multiplied by six;
whatever is obtained are the parvas, and half of that shall be the lunar day (tithi).
This applies to the period beginning with the bright fortnight of Māgha and ending with the dark fortnight of Pauṣa.
They declare that the knowledge of time for a five-year yuga consists of this:
the third, the ninth, and the full moon of the dark fortnight, as well as the sixth and the twelfth, are said to be the equinoxes (viṣuvān). // 32–33 //
The fast-day (upavasatha) shall be on the fourteenth [lunar day] such that the moon reaches the sky during the day;
when the sun is in Śraviṣṭhā, the rainy season begins on the day of the bright fortnight of Māgha.
Just as the crest is to peacocks, and as jewels are to serpents...
In the same way, among the auxiliary sciences of the Vedas (vedāṅga), Jyotiṣa stands at the head.
